newsitem.title: INDIA: Hope meets cynicism as Kashmiris vote for peace.
newsitem.headline: Hope meets cynicism as Kashmiris vote for peace.

text.p: Farmers and old men near a Himalayan stronghold of separatist guerrillas put aside their fears on Monday to cast ballots on the last day of crucial elections in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir.

The old men at Banihal, 95 km (60 miles) south of the state's summer capital of Srinagar, said they wanted to give peace a chance. But cynical teenagers said they saw no hope in the first local polls after seven years of turbulence.
"I hope this election will bring peace to the valley," said Mohammed Hussain, a 60-year-old farmer, after voting.

Monday's voting for six assembly seats in the district of Doda, 250 km (150 miles) south of Srinagar, was the last phase of a month-long programme of staggered polls. Vote counting was set to begin on Tuesday.
Hazy skies seemed to reflect the subdued mood in Banihal, nestled in a valley watered by small streams. The town lies next to Doda district, long a hotbed of separatist militancy.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda hopes the polls will help restore normalcy in the region, torn since 1990 by a separatist revolt in which more than 20,000 people have died.

Dressed in the kaftan-like Kashmiri "pheran" and woollen peaked cap, Gulam Kadeer Lone, a wrinkled, 50-year-old teacher, said: "I'm voting only for peace. I don't mind who the candidate is, who wins or who forms this government."
Most shops were closed except for a couple of tea stalls. Roads were deserted except for groups of people outside polling stations looking for their names on voters' lists.
Many of the dozens of Kashmiri separatist groups who advocate independence or union with Islamic Pakistan have hide-outs in Doda's difficult terrain, police say.
People trickled slowly into the polling booths, heavily guarded by paramilitary troopers, some of them standing on top of the buildings holding automatic weapons.
Police were taking no chances after a blast ripped through the town on Sunday evening. No one was injured.
Many hoped the elections would help reduce the bloodshed.
"It will ease pressure on us from pro-government and separatist militants. We want to live in peace. That's our priority," said Mohammed Aslam Khan, a 38-year-old tourist department employee.
Khan said his favourite candidate was independent Farooq Mir. "We have not seen any politician in the last seven years. Whenever we were in trouble he would come and help us."
Youth seemed less hopeful that good times would return.

Shabbir Ahmed, a 24-year-old science student at Kashmir University, said: "I'm not voting. It makes no difference. We have seen it in the past. I don't think these elections are going to change the situation in Kashmir."
Very few women were seen voting.
Farhat Abbas, a 60-year-old farmer, was gasping for breath by the time he reached the Birshapura polling station on a hilltop. He had clambered up a narrow track with a stick.
"I lost my son-in-law, the only support, in an encounter between the armed forces and the militants," Abbas said as he clutched the arm of a security officer for support.
"I cannot bear to see others facing all these things. I'm voting just to stop the bloodshed."
